analysis.title: FOMC Preview: A Hike Is Now "Unfathomable"... So How Does Warsh Explain Skipping After A Hot CPI?
key_insights: 94 of 100 economists in the latest Reuters poll expect the Fed to hold at 3.75-4.00% on Wednesday Oct 28. Swaps price about 3bp of hike premium and CME FedWatch implies roughly 10%. Goldman's equity vol desk puts swaps-implied odds at 7%.
All 100 poll respondents expect a hike in December. About 60% see the cycle peaking at 4.00-4.25% and about 40% expect at least two more hikes.

Market pricing is more hawkish than the economists. Goldman Marquee shows 3.1bp for this meeting, 24bp by December, 52bp by March and a peak of 75bp of additional tightening by September 2027, taking the effective rate to about 4.63%. Goldman economists expect one more hike in December and then cuts.

Hike premium for the October meeting fell from the mid-teens after the September hike to under 3bp and migrated almost entirely to December. A hot September CPI briefly made October a coin toss before the neocloud selloff and Fed speakers cut the odds.

September CPI was hot. Core rose 0.3% M/M against 0.2% consensus, annual core went to 2.6% from 2.4%, and headline rose 0.6% M/M and 3.7% Y/Y against a 3.6% forecast. PPI and import prices were also hotter than expected.

ANZ notes the three-month annualized core CPI pace rose to 3.4% from 2.0%, supercore services averaged 0.37% M/M in Q3 against 0.17% in Q2, and core goods rose 0.25% M/M, the fastest since January 2025.

September payrolls were 29K, below all estimates, with net revisions of -60K to July and August and unemployment at 4.2%. The article attributes the miss mostly to seasonal adjustment. GDPNow tracks Q3 at 3.5%, claims are near cycle lows and October consumer confidence was 91.7 against 81.0 consensus.

Friday's September core PCE is the key data point. Goldman expects 0.34% and ANZ says even 0.3% lifts the annual rate to 3.1% from 2.8%. JPMorgan's Feroli says Warsh must explain hiking after a 0.2% core PCE print in September but holding after an expected 0.3% print.

Fed speakers point to a compromise of hiking every other meeting. Williams saw no urgency to act in October, Jefferson said more time may be needed, and Waller said hikes need not come at consecutive meetings. FOMC minutes showed all 19 officials backed the September hike and most saw another by year end.
Hawks want more. Hammack favors smaller, quicker adjustments, Logan sees at least 50bp more needed, and Collins (not a voter) sees a greater chance of inflation staying notably above 2%.

ANZ's Brian Martin is the lone prominent October-hike advocate. He cites a real fed funds rate of 0.3% on headline PCE and 0.7% on core, below neutral estimates of 1.0% (NY Fed) and 1.85% (Richmond Fed), an NFCI that has barely tightened, and a historical pattern of sequential hikes once cycles start (2015 the exception).

Political overlay: the meeting is six days before the midterms and the president has said Warsh should have voted against September's hike. Timiraos says a surprise hike before the midterms would be a significant market jolt, and Natixis says avoiding one insulates the Fed from White House criticism.

Statement: Goldman suggests language borrowed from Jefferson that further adjustments will depend on trends in the data, the evolving outlook and the balance of risks. If Warsh sees that as forward guidance, the alternative is to say nothing on the outlook. Feroli expects wording that policy will deliver a timely return to price stability.

Dissents: Rabobank and Natixis expect Hammack, Kashkari and Logan to dissent again for a 25bp hike, as in July. JPMorgan's Feroli expects two (Hammack and Logan) with risk that Kashkari also dissents.

Press conference risk: Goldman's Cahill notes Warsh's most dovish answers in July came when asked why the Fed was not hiking, and that presser triggered the first leg of the long-bond selloff. Marshall says more inflation airtime keeps the front end selling off and flattening, while more airtime on tighter financial conditions re-steepens the curve.

Goldman's case for the hiking cycle ending in December: financial conditions tightened about 30bp, roughly one hike's worth against four priced. Tariffs, the Iran energy shock and mismeasured AI price pressures explain all of core PCE's 1.1pp overshoot, and core PCE should slide toward 2.2% by end-2027.

Energy is the Goldman risk. The oil shock has added 0.3pp to core PCE with 0.1-0.15pp more in the baseline. Oil futures above Goldman's forecast would add another 0.1pp to core PCE by March and about 0.4pp to headline, so a March hike is possible. Oil hit six-month highs on fears of new US and Israeli strikes on Iran before WTI slid back below $100 Tuesday.

San Francisco Fed data highlighted by Apollo's Slok show core PCE inflation at 3% is now split evenly between supply and demand, whereas supply dominated in 2022. Rates can cool demand-driven inflation but not supply shocks, which challenges Goldman's wait-it-out view.

Goldman rates desks: short macro trader Bingham calls an October hike unfathomable and expects a hawkish hold, with 23bp priced for December leaving little room for error. Government trading expects 10Y at 4.80-5.30% and likes buying dips and steepeners into flattening moves. Treasury trading says a 15bp move is more likely a rally extension than a selloff. Strategy keeps positioning for belly outperformance.

Goldman FX: the options market prices a 45bp FOMC move, which looks rich, so owning ATM vol is hard to justify without a Warsh slip. They prefer cheap USD skew via front-end GBPUSD risk reversals, favor selective USD strength, see EUR heavy with scope to retest 1.1113, would sell USDJPY into a post-BOJ rally and would sell USDCAD ahead of a hawkish BOC.

Goldman equity derivatives: index vol and skew are historically elevated YTD ahead of FOMC, Mag 7 earnings and midterms. The desk likes SPX put spreads for a selloff and says calls are cheap enough to own outright. The S&P has closed lower on every FOMC day this year.

Goldman macro, credit and commodities: Chang says the bar for Warsh to sound hawkish relative to pricing is high and a post-FOMC, post-big-tech patch may be friendlier for risk, but she wants upside in protected form. Credit favors CDX HY over IG tactically, with CDX IG exposed to volatility in IG AI CDS. Commodities see oil's back end outperforming with front vol and call skew finding a bid.

Historical check from Goldman: across nine tightening cycles since the early 1980s, stocks struggle initially then recover and yields keep rising with a flatter curve. 1997 and 2015 were one-and-done, others delivered at least 175bp. In 1999 the Fed hiked into an investment boom and the S&P stayed rangebound before the tech bubble burst.

Base case is a hawkish hold, a statement leaving the door open for December, a short presser and possibly three dissents. Fed-induced volatility may extend into next week as the midterms land, and the BOC (Wednesday), ECB and BOJ (Thursday) also report. The author expects central banks to hike less than priced given AI credit stress, a soft labor market and $100 oil.

risk_factors: Warsh press conference slip: dovish answers on why the Fed is not hiking triggered the long-bond selloff in July, and dwelling on the hold while giving no path could repeat it.
Unexplained hold less than a week before the midterms could fuel perceptions that policy is driven by non-economic considerations (Feroli).
Hotter than expected September core PCE on Friday (0.3% or higher) would strengthen the hawks.
Oil above Goldman's forecast could add about 0.1pp to core PCE by March and about 0.4pp to headline, making a March hike possible.
Demand-driven inflation: with core PCE at 3% split evenly between supply and demand, waiting out the overshoot may not work.
AI drawdown or AI credit stress could trigger a front-end led torque steepener.
Escalation with Iran after the midterms, with Iran threatening Gulf energy assets.
Three hawkish dissents (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) at a compromise meeting.
Little room for error with 23-24bp priced for December.
Comparison with 1999: hiking into an investment boom with high valuations preceded a tech bubble burst.
charts_described: Goldman Marquee chart shows October hike premium falling from the mid-teens after the September hike to under 3bp while December premium rose.
Goldman chart shows the S&P 500 closing lower on every FOMC day this year, barely so in January and April.
Goldman Marquee chart shows the 10Y Treasury sitting right at 5%.
vol_and_positioning: FX options price a 45bp move for the FOMC, which Goldman FX says looks rich relative to historical meetings.
Index vol and skew remain at historically elevated levels on a YTD lookback heading into the FOMC, Mag 7 earnings and midterms.
The S&P 500 has closed lower on every FOMC day this year, barely so in January and April.
Rates positioning: consensus is short 2x z6 versus long 1x z7. The most painful quadrant for most participants is a torque steepener led by the front contract if the AI drawdown worsens sharply.
CTAs remain short duration, hedge funds are light after unwinding duration longs (mostly in Europe), and real money has moved from underweight to less underweight.
CDX IG was insulated by gamma into this week's expiry, but most of that is rolling off, leaving it exposed to volatility in IG AI CDS.
Oil front vol and call skew found a bid after months of selling off to below pre-war levels.
geopolitical: Fears of a more violent new wave of US and Israeli strikes on Iran, possibly before the midterms, pushed oil to six-month highs, with Iran threatening to retaliate against energy assets across the Gulf.
Goldman rates trader notes consensus positioning is built on the view that Trump re-escalates Middle East tensions as soon as the midterms pass.
Tariffs and the Iran energy shock are cited by Goldman as drivers of the core PCE overshoot.
The midterm elections six days after the FOMC, and presidential criticism of Warsh's September hike, are cited as political overlay for the decision.
cross_bank_references: Goldman economists remain the most dovish shop on the Street, expecting one more hike in December then cuts, versus market pricing of about three more.
ANZ's Martin favors a 25bp October hike against the Natixis, Goldman and JPMorgan base cases of a hold.
Rabobank and Natixis expect all three hawkish dissents again, JPMorgan's Feroli expects two with risk of a third.
Natixis expects a brief press conference without follow-up questions, Goldman economists do not expect significant new information.
ING thinks Warsh will avoid suggesting wider credit spreads and weaker stocks reduce the need for hikes.
JPMorgan did not publish its usual Fed-day scenario matrix this month.

tension_points.bull_case: Hawks (ANZ's Martin, Hammack, Logan) argue September core CPI did not show inflation moving to target at sufficient speed, real rates are below neutral, financial conditions have barely tightened, and past cycles hiked at sequential meetings.
tension_points.bear_case: Williams, Jefferson, Waller and Bowman signaled no urgency, the minutes pointed to December, September payrolls were weak, and a surprise hike before the midterms would be a market jolt and draw White House criticism.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A hot September core PCE print of 0.3% or more on Friday, or a Warsh statement or presser signaling a bias to hike, would revive December or earlier hike risk.

tension_points.theme: Goldman two-and-done versus market four hikes
tension_points.bull_case: Goldman says the core PCE overshoot is fully explained by supply shocks that fade, financial conditions have tightened about 30bp, and inflation will largely have to be waited out, so hikes end in December and cuts follow.
tension_points.bear_case: The SF Fed data show half of core PCE inflation is demand-driven, which rates can cool but waiting cannot, and the market's four hikes may not be so crazy. Oil above Goldman's forecast adds to core PCE.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Goldman concedes a March hike is possible if inflation numbers are worse than it expects, including a bigger January effect from companies passing on higher costs.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman's Bingham expects a hawkish hold and Feroli suggests Warsh say the Committee is biased to hike, which would anchor December pricing.
tension_points.bear_case: Warsh refuses forward guidance and in July his dovish answers came when explaining why the Fed was not hiking, which triggered a long-bond selloff.
tension_points.what_invalidates: More time spent on inflation flattens the curve and sells off the front end, while more time on tighter financial conditions re-steepens the curve (Goldman's Marshall).

theme_stances.key_argument: Fedspeak points to a compromise of hiking every other meeting, skipping October and hiking in December.
theme_stances.evidence: December, in other words, is the compromise.

theme_stances.key_argument: Goldman says the inflation overshoot from past supply shocks will largely have to be waited out and financial conditions have already tightened.
theme_stances.evidence: the inflation overshoot caused by past supply shocks will largely have to be waited out

theme_stances.key_argument: If half of inflation is demand-driven, it probably cannot all be waited out and the market's four hikes may be justified.
theme_stances.evidence: interest rates can cool demand-driven inflation but do little about supply shocks
